newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee higher, talk of output decline.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee higher, talk of output decline.

text.p: Indonesian Robusta coffee prices were higher on Monday, with increasing talk of a decline in production due to bad weather, traders said.
The local price was quoted at 3,350-3,400 rupiah/kg in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra, compared with 3,300-3,500 rupiah a week ago.
The traders said the export price was $1,450-$1,500/tonne FOB Lampung, up from $1,400-$1,450 last Monday.
"Local prices are still relatively high," one trader said. "Supply is still tight although more beans are beginning to enter the market as the harvest proceeds."
The traders said they expected London coffee futures to open $30 a tonne lower when it opens later on Monday.

"London is likely to take the lead from New York, which closed lower last Friday," one trader said. "Although some traders feel London could open lower by as much as $50, I think it will be down by around $30 at the opening."
New York coffee prices ended broadly lower for the second straight session last Friday on profit taking.
London prices, however, rebounded from their lows last Friday on late short-covering, with May finishing just $1 down at $1,729 a tonne after a touching a session low of $1,670.
Indonesian traders said there was talk that domestic production could be hit by bad weather, which affected the flowering process in several growing areas.
But their estimate of the expected production drop ranged from 20 percent to as high as 40 percent.

"My company's estimate is that production will fall by a conservative 20 percent this year," one trader said. "Heavy rains caused flowers to drop, and not all trees had a second flowering. Strong winds also affected the flowering."
He said the bad weather might also cause a delay in harvesting in some areas on Sumatra Island.
Another trader said he had been getting reports from growers that output might drop by as much as 40 percent.
"Growers are saying they expect production to fall quite sharply this year because of heavy rains that affected flowering," the trader said.
"One grower whose fields produced some 9,000 tonnes last year is looking to harvest only 3,500 to 4,000 tonnes this year. Another said his output could fall by 40 percent."
But another trader dismissed talk of severe production falls as "nonsense", saying declines could be about 10 to 15 percent.
He said some coffee areas were affected by bad weather, but added that production in others had not been affected.
"When coffee prices rose in 1994, there were a lot of new plantings," he said. "And these trees are now bearing fruit.

"The younger trees will produce much more than the older ones and will help make up for declines in production in the areas hit by bad weather," he said. "I expect overall output to be down by between 10 to 15 percent."
Traders also said an agreement by African producers to share 850,000-bags in export cuts was unlikely to have any significant impact on the market.

"The news is welcomed but I don't think it will lead to an increase in prices," one said. The African move was part of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' (ACPC) plan to further cut exports in the first half of this year.
Traders said a move by Colombia to raise its internal coffee price could help support prices. "I think it should be supportive," one trader said.
Colombian internal coffee prices have shot up 62 percent since the start of the year as the authorities try to bring them in line with world prices.
-- K.T. Arasu, Jakarta newsroom + 6221 384-6364
